topic.name: The Shortest Distance Between a Plane and a Point

question.text: Given that $Q(2, 4, 1)$ lies on the plane $\Pi:\mathbf{r} \cdot \langle -6,2,9 \rangle =5 $, find the shortest distance from $P(6, -1, 0)$ to $\Pi.$
question.explanation:
First, we find \begin{align*} \overrightarrow{PQ} &= \langle 2,4,1 \rangle - \langle 6, -1, 0\rangle \\[3pt] &= \langle -4, 5,1 \rangle. \end{align*}

From the equation of the plane, we get the normal vector $\mathbf{n}= \langle -6,2,9 \rangle.$

Finally, the shortest distance from the point $P$ to the plane $\Pi$ is the absolute value of the scalar projection of $\overrightarrow{PQ}$ onto the normal vector of the plane:

\begin{align*} d &= | \text{comp}_{\mathbf{n}} \, \overrightarrow{PQ} | \\[5pt] &= \dfrac{| \overrightarrow{PQ} \cdot \mathbf{n} |}{|\mathbf{n}|} \\[5pt] &= \dfrac{| (-4)\cdot(-6)+5\cdot2+1\cdot9 |}{\sqrt{(-6)^2+2^2+9^2}} \\[5pt] &= \dfrac{|24+10+9|}{\sqrt{36+4+81}} \\[5pt] &= \dfrac{|43|}{\sqrt{121}} \\[5pt] &= \dfrac{43}{11} \end{align*}

question.text: Find the shortest distance between the point $P(5, 4, -4)$ and the plane $\Pi$ with equation $6x-3y+6z=-18.$
question.explanation:
Let's start by picking a point on the plane. To do that, we simply substitute some concrete values for $x$ and $y$ into the equation and solve for $z.$ Let's choose $x=1$ and $y=2$ (though it doesn't really matter what values we choose). Solving for $z,$ we get

\begin{align*} 6x-3y+6z&= -18 \\[3pt] 6(1)-3(2)+6z &= -18 \\[3pt] 6z &= -18 \\[3pt] z &= -3. \end{align*}

So, we get the point $Q(1,2,-3)$ which lies on the plane.

Computing $\overrightarrow{PQ},$ we get

\begin{align*} \overrightarrow{PQ} &= \langle 1,2,-3 \rangle - \langle 5, 4, -4 \rangle \\[3pt] &= \langle -4, -2, 1 \rangle. \end{align*}

We also need a normal vector to the plane. For any Cartesian equation of a plane $ax+by+cz=d,$ the normal vector is $\mathbf{n}=\langle a,b,c \rangle.$ So, for the plane $\Pi,$ we have $\mathbf{n}= \langle 6,-3, 6 \rangle.$

Finally, the shortest distance from the point $P$ to the plane $\Pi$ is the absolute value of the scalar projection of $\overrightarrow{PQ}$ onto the normal vector of the plane:

\begin{align*} d &= | \text{comp}_{\mathbf{n}} \, \overrightarrow{PQ} | \\[5pt] &= \dfrac{| \overrightarrow{PQ} \cdot \mathbf{n} |}{|\mathbf{n}|} \\[5pt] &= \dfrac{| (-4) \cdot 6 + (-2) \cdot (-3) + 1 \cdot 6 |}{\sqrt{6^2+(-3)^2+6^2}} \\[5pt] &= \dfrac{|-24+6+6|}{\sqrt{36+9+36}} \\[5pt] &= \dfrac{|\,-12\,|}{\sqrt{81}} \\[5pt] &= \dfrac{4}{3} \end{align*}

question.text: Find the shortest distance between the point $P(-11 , -8 , -4)$ and the plane $\Pi$ with equation $14x+8y-8z = -6.$
question.explanation:
Let's start by picking a point on the plane. To do that, we simply substitute some concrete values for $x$ and $y$ into the equation and solve for $z.$ Let's choose $x=-1$ and $y=-2$ (though it doesn't really matter what values we choose). Solving for $z,$ we get

\begin{align*} 14x+8y-8z &= -6 \\[3pt] 14(-1)+8(-2)-8z &= -6 \\[3pt] -8z &= 24 \\[3pt] z &= -3. \end{align*}

So, we get the point $Q(-1, -2, -3)$ which lies on the plane.

Computing $\overrightarrow{PQ},$ we get

\begin{align*} \overrightarrow{PQ} &= \langle -1 , -2 , -3 \rangle - \langle -11 , -8 , -4 \rangle \\[3pt] &= \langle 10 , 6 , 1 \rangle. \end{align*}

We also need a normal vector to the plane. For any Cartesian equation of a plane $ax+by+cz=d,$ the normal vector is $\mathbf{n}=\langle a,b,c \rangle.$ So, for the plane $\Pi,$ we have $\mathbf{n}= \langle 14, 8, -8 \rangle.$

Finally, the shortest distance from the point $P$ to the plane $\Pi$ is the absolute value of the scalar projection of $\overrightarrow{PQ}$ onto the normal vector of the plane:

\begin{align*} d &= | \text{comp}_{\mathbf{n}} \, \overrightarrow{PQ} | \\[5pt] &= \dfrac{| \overrightarrow{PQ} \cdot \mathbf{n} |}{|\mathbf{n}|} \\[5pt] &= \dfrac{| 10 \cdot 14 + 6 \cdot 8 + 1 \cdot (-8) |}{\sqrt{(14)^2+8^2+(-8)^2}} \\[5pt] &= \dfrac{|140+48-8|}{\sqrt{196+64+64}} \\[5pt] &= \dfrac{|\,180\,|}{\sqrt{324}} \\[5pt] &= 10 \end{align*}

question.text: Given that $Q(4,-2,8)$ lies on the plane $\Pi:\mathbf{r} \cdot \langle -3,6,2\rangle =-8 $, find the shortest distance from $P(3,-4,2)$ to $\Pi.$
question.explanation:
First, we find

\begin{align*} \overrightarrow{PQ} &= \langle 4,-2,8 \rangle - \langle 3,-4,2 \rangle \\[3pt] &= \langle 1, 2, 6 \rangle. \end{align*}

From the equation of the plane, we get the normal vector $\mathbf{n}= \langle -3,6,2 \rangle.$

Finally, the shortest distance from the point $P$ to the plane $\Pi$ is the absolute value of the scalar projection of $\overrightarrow{PQ}$ onto the normal vector of the plane:

\begin{align*} d &= | \text{comp}_{\mathbf{n}} \, \overrightarrow{PQ} | \\[5pt] &= \dfrac{| \overrightarrow{PQ} \cdot \mathbf{n} |}{|\mathbf{n}|} \\[5pt] &= \dfrac{| 1 \cdot (-3)+2 \cdot 6 + 6 \cdot 2 |}{\sqrt{(-3)^2+6^2+2^2}} \\[5pt] &= \dfrac{|-3+12+12|}{\sqrt{9+36+4}} \\[5pt] &= \dfrac{|21|}{\sqrt{49}} \\[5pt] &= \dfrac{21}{7} \\[5pt] &= 3. \end{align*}

question.text: Given that $Q(5,-1,9)$ lies on the plane $\Pi:\mathbf{r} \cdot \langle 3, -6,-2 \rangle = 3$, find the shortest distance from $P(7,-2,8)$ to $\Pi.$
question.explanation:
First, we find

\begin{align*} \overrightarrow{PQ} &= \langle 5,-1,9 \rangle - \langle 7,-2,8\rangle \\[3pt] &= \langle -2, 1, 1 \rangle. \end{align*}

From the equation of a plane, we get a normal vector $\mathbf{n}= \langle 3,-6,-2 \rangle.$

Finally, the shortest distance from the point $P$ to the plane $\Pi$ is the absolute value of the scalar projection of $\overrightarrow{PQ}$ onto the normal vector of the plane:

\begin{align*} d &= | \text{comp}_{\mathbf{n}} \, \overrightarrow{PQ} | \\[5pt] &= \dfrac{| \overrightarrow{PQ} \cdot \mathbf{n} |}{|\mathbf{n}|} \\[5pt] &= \dfrac{| (-2) \cdot 3 + 1 \cdot (-6) + 1 \cdot (-2) |}{\sqrt{3^2+(-6)^2+(-2)^2}} \\[5pt] &= \dfrac{|-6-6-2|}{\sqrt{9+36+4}} \\[5pt] &= \dfrac{|-14|}{\sqrt{49}} \\[5pt] &= \dfrac{14}{7} \\[5pt] &= 2. \end{align*}
